desert_p04_001.speaker: narrator
desert_p04_001.text: Gao stopped at the southern end of the causeway and called Tuo back from the middle. The water against its northern face had reached beneath a row of stones. The old woman said it had risen since yesterday, when her grandson could stand dry beside the central block. Her companion put down the fodder and showed where the block had tilted. Under a person's weight it moved only slightly. Under a loaded water cart, that slight movement could become another kind of journey.

desert_p04_002.speaker: narrator
desert_p04_002.text: Han watched from the approach with his hands clasped behind him, keeping his impatience where everybody could see it. The old woman had brought a narrow plank for her foot crossing. She did not offer it to the caravan. Tuo asked whether the western grass route still connected with the northern road. It did, though the farm collective had closed its inner lane after a bullock broke the ditch bank. The outer track remained firm enough for carts. The woman studied their wheels and asked whether they were carrying stone.

desert_p04_003.speaker: narrator
desert_p04_003.text: Han named water, grain, survey equipment, and the ordinary necessities of twelve people. She said water could weigh more awkwardly than stone, because it chose its own moments to move.

desert_p04_004.speaker: gao_ru
desert_p04_004.text: We shall not load this causeway today. I can measure the displaced stones, but that does not make me the person who can promise their foundations will hold. The northern edge has lost support, and the water conceals how much. Take the carts back to the firm approach. Leave room for the fodder carriers to cross on foot. Tuo and I will look at the western route with somebody who uses it. Han, you may dislike the lost time aloud once. After that I need your attention on choosing a road, not on mourning the road we expected.

desert_p04_005.speaker: narrator
desert_p04_005.text: Han said the word he had chosen was unsuited to the company and would remain private. The old woman laughed for the first time. Her companion volunteered to show the western track after carrying his fodder across. He made two trips rather than stacking the whole load on his shoulders. Yue held the cloth bundle at the approach, careful of her palms, and listened as the woman identified the grass by its smell. This cutting would feed calves. The thicker crop nearer the water would become roof mats, provided the quarry's pale sediment did not spoil its fibres before harvest.

desert_p04_006.speaker: narrator
desert_p04_006.text: Yue had expected salt to end cultivation. Here green roots lived beside white crust, and every change in water altered somebody's work. The woman noticed her curiosity and tore a small stem to show its pith. Her name would matter to the collective's record, she said, but travellers generally called her Auntie Reed. Yue asked about the tall grass instead of pressing for the woman's private name. The woman offered a scrap of stem to chew and warned her not to swallow the fibres. It tasted faintly sweet.

desert_p04_007.speaker: narrator
desert_p04_007.text: Beyond the causeway, the fodder carrier waited with his last load balanced against a hip. Gao sent Yue back to watch the carts while she and Tuo inspected the outer track. The girl found the cook arranging his stove box so he could reach the midday meal without unloading everything. He claimed he had foreseen a delay through the beans' expression at breakfast. Bao made him share the dried greens with the drivers before anyone had an excuse to forget eating. Du stood beside the eastern approach, comparing the fallen sign's approximate position with his old distances.

desert_p04_008.speaker: narrator
desert_p04_008.text: He did not try to cross the causeway. His hands moved over the map as if feeling for a hidden seam.

desert_p04_009.speaker: du_she
desert_p04_009.text: The original road crossed here when the northern channel stayed behind its bank. My father bought fodder from this farm on that camel journey. I remember a boy selling us a basket of white eggs, and my father's insistence that one was stone. The boy swore it was merely a very reserved egg. I could put that story in a map margin and it would still tell us nothing useful about today's foundations. Yet memory keeps offering it instead of the measure I need. People praise an old man for remembering. They seldom ask whether he remembers the right thing.

desert_p04_010.speaker: narrator
desert_p04_010.text: Yue asked whether the stone egg had proved edible. Du said it had proved an excellent weight for his father's letters. The answer made them both smile. He then showed her the channel's older outline, printed from a survey made before the quarry settling basin. The bank had been marked as seasonal, not permanent. Later sheets had simplified it to a firm boundary because carriers wanted clearer instructions. He had accepted that simplification. Today the water ran across it.

desert_p04_011.speaker: narrator
desert_p04_011.text: Yue copied both outlines into separate sketches, understanding why a clean line could become an untidy promise without anybody explicitly making one. Tuo returned first, carrying a strand of dark grass tangled around her staff cap. The outer track added distance but stood on a low gravel ridge. Its narrowest turn would require the carts one at a time, with the rack folded again. Gao remained at the collective's western shed to ask about a damaged culvert farther along. No loaded crossing would be attempted without looking.

desert_p04_012.speaker: narrator
desert_p04_012.text: Han listened, breathed once, and offered the farm payment for any crop damaged by their wheels outside the established track. Auntie Reed said she preferred keeping the wheels on the track to negotiating a price for flattened winter feed.

desert_p04_013.speaker: han_xun
desert_p04_013.text: So do I. Show my drivers the edges you mean, and we shall have them walk the narrow turn before taking a team through. If a wheel goes beyond it, we will stop and settle what happened before leaving. I am not offering money as a licence to be careless. The road carriers will also need your report about this causeway. May I leave a copy of our sketch here when it is finished? You can add your own account to the waterkeeper's letter.

desert_p04_014.speaker: han_xun
desert_p04_014.text: A message from an expensive map man should not be the only one anybody bothers to read.

desert_p04_015.speaker: narrator
desert_p04_015.text: Du lifted his head at the title, considered protesting, and decided Han had not exaggerated his price. Auntie Reed accepted the sketch and said the collective had already sent two letters about the quarry bank. The first received a promise of inspection; the second received a request to use the correct form. She had kept both replies under a cracked bowl, where they protected the shelf from damp cups. Bao suggested their eventual practical use might be greater than the office had intended. The woman nodded gravely and asked whether clinicians were allowed to write rude comments on public forms.

desert_p04_016.speaker: narrator
desert_p04_016.text: Gao returned with the outer route sketched in her field book. The damaged culvert carried only a handcart lane, which the caravan would avoid. The main track's recent wheel marks had come from two fodder carts of comparable width, though neither had their water load. Its gravel surface and banks were visible along the approach. Tuo would walk the narrow turn while the first cart waited. They could proceed slowly without using the flooded causeway. Han told the drivers, who accepted the plan more readily than he had. Waiting beside an obviously tilted stone had made the choice plain.

desert_p04_017.speaker: narrator
desert_p04_017.text: Yue packed the rods before walking back to the gravel junction. The old woman called her once, handing over a short woven band. It could fasten the grass sample without crushing it into the notebook. Yue said she had no reason to take the sample away if the woman wanted it. Auntie Reed waved at acres of stems. She wanted the girl to remember that white ground did not mean empty ground. Yue thanked her and put the little bundle in the outside pocket. The sweet taste lingered in her mouth after they had left the causeway behind.

desert_p04_018.speaker: narrator
desert_p04_018.text: The narrow turn lay between two banks faced with reeds. Tuo marked its safe outer edge using the collective's existing posts. Gao watched the first cart's wheel path from the higher ground. Long Legs brought the team through a pace at a time, waiting for Tuo's hand signal before turning. The folded rack stayed clear of the bank. On the second cart, a mule reached toward a reed fringe and pulled the lead taut. Its driver halted, settled the animal, and resumed. Nobody shouted.

desert_p04_019.speaker: narrator
desert_p04_019.text: Yue discovered that slow work could feel more urgent than a runaway cart because every movement offered time to imagine its failure. The equipment cart followed with its quiet driver watching both rear corners. The last wheel cleared the turn by a modest span of gravel. Gao had Yue measure that visible clearance after the cart stood straight, not while it moved. It would help later carriers know what vehicle width the track had actually admitted. The figure belonged to today's route and condition, not every future load. Du added the date beside it.

desert_p04_020.speaker: narrator
desert_p04_020.text: On the bank a child watching from a shed applauded as though they had performed a trick. The driver bowed with one hand still firmly around the brake lever. Beyond the turn lay a village of low houses around a grass-drying yard. Bundles hung from rails, their cut ends glowing gold in the morning light. A man repairing a roof mat called Tuo by name and asked whether she still cheated at tiles. She said only against people who deserved instruction. He offered the caravan shade in the outer yard for its next rest.

desert_p04_021.speaker: narrator
desert_p04_021.text: Han accepted after checking that the carts would not block the drying rails. Yue saw the same attention to space that had begun at the gate, each person making room for work already happening rather than arriving as its centre. The villagers had heard the culvert report from the quarry rider the previous day. Nobody expected him to carry their argument back as well. They had chosen a separate messenger, waiting for the midday wagon toward Bitter Wells. Gao offered the causeway sketch as another enclosure, dated and signed.

desert_p04_022.speaker: narrator
desert_p04_022.text: Du gave them a corrected public sheet without his private customer notes. The roof-mat maker studied the northern channel and said the old line was the one his grandmother had taught him to fear. He traced it with a blunt finger, then showed Gao where the current spill had reached the drying ground.

desert_p04_023.speaker: gao_ru
desert_p04_023.text: Let us draw that edge while we can still see it. A week from now the damp mark may be gone, and everybody will be arguing about how far the water came. Yue, hold the book while he points; you need not step into the crop. I shall write his description beside the visible stain. Our customer ordered a road survey. The water moving beside that road affects its people too. We can include a short observation without pretending we have measured the quarry's entire drainage scheme. Du, give me the smaller scale. I want the shed in this sketch.

desert_p04_024.speaker: narrator
desert_p04_024.text: They worked from the yard's edge. The spill had left a pale fan of sediment among the grass roots, distinct from the older salt crust farther out. Gao sampled it into two paper packets from her kit, keeping one for the collective if they wanted examination later. Yue labelled the place and time. She was surprised by how gently the roof-mat maker held the packet. His crop had become something an office could misunderstand in the palm of a hand.

desert_p04_025.speaker: narrator
desert_p04_025.text: Bao came out with lunch bowls and waited until the writing was finished before putting one where Gao could smell it. The caravan paid for the yard's use, a bucket from the village's separate washing supply, and a small bundle of fodder inspected by the farrier. Their road drinking water remained in the tanks; the wash bucket never entered its count. Han wrote the purchase on a plain receipt the mat maker could read. The cook asked for one roof-mat offcut to shield the stove from the breeze.

desert_p04_026.speaker: narrator
desert_p04_026.text: The maker gave him a damaged piece and received dried fruit in return. Their trade required no map. Yue watched the stove's smoke improve while the reed fibres shifted overhead like quiet hands. During lunch a villager brought out a repaired string instrument with a shallow wooden body. He played while tying knots in the mat frame, using the pauses to check their tension. Tuo complained that his old fast tune had slowed. He said it was for old people eating, and she should hurry her bowl if offended. Gao tapped the rhythm on her knee.

desert_p04_027.speaker: narrator
desert_p04_027.text: Du hummed under his breath, initially out of time, then found it. The drivers listened with their hats off. For a little while the detour had acquired something worth remembering beyond its lost miles.

desert_p04_028.speaker: tuo_yin
desert_p04_028.text: When I was young I danced to that tune at a wedding and broke the heel off somebody's very expensive shoe. Nobody recalls who married. Everybody recalls the shoe. The owner forgave me after three years, by which time I had developed a useful habit of keeping away from heels. These villagers remember things generously when they want you to stay, and exactly when they want you to pay. You can trust the causeway account. Three different families would fight over the date of a feast and still agree on which stone their calves fell beside.

desert_p04_029.speaker: narrator
desert_p04_029.text: Yue asked whether Tuo had guided through the village with her brother. The woman nodded without looking away from the player. They had carried salt fish north and mat bundles south. Her brother liked this halt because he could dance without a partner complaining about freight schedules. One summer he had borrowed the instrument for a camp song and forgotten to return it until winter. The player heard his name in the conversation and held the tune a little longer at its final note. Tuo finished her bowl.

desert_p04_030.speaker: narrator
desert_p04_030.text: Neither offered the ending of that older journey, and Yue did not require it. The next stretch climbed from the village onto the gravel ridge. Han paid the yard keeper and thanked the player, who demanded his thanks be delivered by somebody who could recognise the tune. Gao obliged with an accurate whistle. Du looked mildly wounded, though the player shook his hand as well. Yue returned the wash bucket, tied the woven grass band more firmly, and followed Tuo out past the drying rails. The smell of fresh stems gave way to sun-warmed salt.

desert_p04_031.speaker: narrator
desert_p04_031.text: Behind them, the mat maker lifted Gao's sketch above his children's reach and slipped it into the collective's message bundle. The ridge proved rougher than its entrance. Old wheel ruts cut diagonally across newer ones, and exposed gravel rolled under the cart rims. The drivers took turns easing their brakes on the steeper portions. Yue walked outside the wheel track with her staff planted ahead. Her healing palms allowed its light support; they would not have tolerated gripping a loaded rope. On the second rise Han offered her a seat beside the cook for a short interval.

desert_p04_032.speaker: narrator
desert_p04_032.text: She accepted, discovering that fatigue could arrive without any dramatic collapse and that accepting rest was easier when nobody turned it into a test. From the cart seat the basin opened northward, pale and broad beneath a sky too clear to soften it. A line of dark stones marked the road's higher edge. Beyond them, silver grass grew in a narrow seam that Tuo called the buried channel. The grass did not promise drinkable water or a safe well. It showed where roots found moisture below the surface. Yue held that distinction without writing it immediately.

desert_p04_033.speaker: narrator
desert_p04_033.text: The cook offered a fragment of preserved pear. She ate it slowly, feeling the cart's sway change at every wheel hollow, and tried not to spill the sweetness into her lap. Gao stopped the line at a wide gravel shoulder to compare the ridge with the old public sheet. The route had shifted west since its last measured edition, following a bank repair. Du's correction slips would need another note. He pressed his fingers against the bridge of his spectacles, then nodded. Yue helped unfold the tripod while Tuo checked the forward track.

desert_p04_034.speaker: narrator
desert_p04_034.text: The shaded bubble took longer to settle than it had in the yard. Gao let it wait. Behind them the drivers poured the mules' measured rest water into low troughs carried on the carts, then returned the troughs to their hooks.

desert_p04_035.speaker: du_she
desert_p04_035.text: A compiler can always find a reason to blame the ground. It moved; the bank failed; the marker vanished; somebody repaired the road without announcing it in good handwriting. Those reasons may all be true. They do not explain why the old edition still looks as certain as the day I drew it. I put the survey date in small type because buyers wanted distance more than history. Now history keeps climbing into the road. Yue, leave space for Gao's new line. I shall make the old date large enough that even Han cannot hide it beneath his thumb.

desert_p04_036.speaker: narrator
desert_p04_036.text: Han, who had been listening while pretending to inspect a harness, said he had never used his thumb to conceal a date. Gao asked about the winter freight estimate. He admitted that had been an index finger. Du laughed and made the new notation. Yue noticed how the jokes allowed them to remain at the table after an uncomfortable truth. They did not make the old sheet more accurate, but they kept its maker willing to change it. The readings agreed within the instrument's working range. Gao closed the sighting head, wiped its cover, and signalled the carts forward.

desert_p04_037.speaker: narrator
desert_p04_037.text: The day's heat strengthened during the final climb. Bao moved along the line at the next halt and added water to the crew's actual portions rather than treating the morning forecast as a prize for endurance. Han recorded the increase. The mules rested beneath the overlapping cart shades, their sides moving steadily. Yue's face had begun to ache from the reflected light; lowering the screens helped. She could still see Tuo's staff ahead and the dark strip of road beneath it.

desert_p04_038.speaker: narrator
desert_p04_038.text: The guide led them toward an old quarry shelter, not yet Crescent House, where the ridge offered a cooler place to camp. A broken pulley hung above the quarry shelter's doorway. Inside, Gao found only two sound walls and a floor littered with blown grit. Tuo chose the open gravel outside instead, where falling masonry could not reach their tents. The camp worker used the sheltered wall as a windbreak without tying anything to its loose upper stones. Yue fetched the flag case and set the last cart's stopping mark.

desert_p04_039.speaker: narrator
desert_p04_039.text: The cook inspected the ruin with professional disappointment: its shade was excellent, its roof nonexistent. Long Legs offered to write a complaint to the former owner. The cook said he already had too many dead customers. As the carts settled, Yue saw a narrow staircase cut into the shelter's northern wall. It ended at a blocked opening, half filled with pale debris. A line of old black letters remained above it, too weathered to read from the yard. She called Du, who studied it while standing outside the fall zone.

desert_p04_040.speaker: narrator
desert_p04_040.text: He recognised the style used by former basin engineers, though not enough surviving words to recover the name. Tuo said Crescent House had similar stairs and would likely be less obliging about rubble. The broken shelter had brought the old road's vanished buildings a little nearer without revealing anything inside them. The water book ended the second day at one thousand five hundred and thirty-three litres. Heat had increased the human portions; the animals had taken their ordinary measured amount. Han wrote the extra use without sighing at anyone's cup.

desert_p04_041.speaker: narrator
desert_p04_041.text: Tuo calculated that an early start could recover part of their lost distance if the next road remained firm. Gao wanted the drivers rested before accepting a longer morning. They spoke beside the first cart, voices low but not secret. Yue sat within hearing, changing the woven band around the grass sample. The green stem had already begun to dry.

desert_p04_042.speaker: han_xun
desert_p04_042.text: If we arrive at Crescent House late on the fourth day, we can do the first exterior work that evening and the rest the following morning. I am asking whether that remains sensible, not announcing that it shall happen. The carriers expect a measured approach and a roof condition report. They do not need every decorative scratch under a stair. Du, I know the old buildings interest you. They interest me too. But the road home remains part of the job, and the report becomes less useful if the people paid to deliver it cannot return.

desert_p04_043.speaker: du_she
desert_p04_043.text: You are accusing me before I have requested a single decorative scratch. That is an improvement in your planning, though an injury to my pleasure. The exterior work may suffice for the carrier report. I should still like to identify the former station correctly. My earliest source calls it Crescent House, the later one calls it the North Exchange. If those are two buildings, we could measure the wrong roof very efficiently. Give us enough daylight to place the site against its landmarks. Curiosity is not the only reason a name matters, even when it happens to be mine.

desert_p04_044.speaker: narrator
desert_p04_044.text: Gao spread the three accounts between them. The site stood against a dark ridge, with a courtyard opening east and a descending stair on its north side. Tuo had seen those features years ago. The carriers' recent sketches showed the ridge but omitted the stair. They would establish the identity before surveying, then choose work from what was actually safe. Bao added that tomorrow's longer morning depended on everyone's condition at dawn. Long Legs, passing with a feed bag, said his condition would improve if the discussion included supper. Han surrendered the table to bowls and postponed the final decision.

desert_p04_045.speaker: narrator
desert_p04_045.text: Yue sat beside the driver with the wooden bird. He took it from its sock and showed her a hollow body painted green, with a little reed inside. His daughter had asked for a bird that could sing in winter. He had bought this one in Bitter Wells and was carrying it to test whether the reed survived road dust. Yue asked why he had not left it at home. He said the child had insisted he learn its song before returning.

desert_p04_046.speaker: narrator
desert_p04_046.text: He blew a note so poor that the cook threatened to classify it as an animal requiring separate feed. The driver tried again more gently. This time a clear, trembling sound crossed the bowls. Tuo smiled without looking up. Du recognised the old dance tune's first interval and added the next with his own whistle. The little bird answered badly, then better. Yue found herself laughing with the driver's effort rather than at it. He had spent the day steering a heavy cart over difficult ground.

desert_p04_047.speaker: narrator
desert_p04_047.text: Beside the stove he concentrated just as seriously on two notes intended for somebody who would meet him at home. The road had room for that obligation as well as the larger printed ones. After supper Bao inspected the camp worker's left wrist. A shelter stake had jarred it when a buried stone turned the hammer. There was swelling but no deformity, and movement remained possible. She bound it, limited tomorrow's striking work, and asked Han to redistribute the stakes among the drivers. The worker looked anxious until Han said his waiting and camp wages remained the same.

desert_p04_048.speaker: narrator
desert_p04_048.text: Yue offered to hold light lines while others drove stakes. Bao agreed if her palms continued closing. The extra work was modest, but the camp would now depend on a slightly different arrangement of hands. The broken shelter wall began to make a faint singing noise as evening wind passed its blocked stair. Yue heard it while clearing bowls and initially mistook it for the wooden bird. The driver lifted both hands to prove his innocence. Gao walked closer, stopping outside the loose masonry.

desert_p04_049.speaker: narrator
desert_p04_049.text: A gap above the stair admitted air through a narrow curved duct, its lower outlet partly covered by grit. When the wind shifted, the note changed. Du brought the lantern and found an old ventilation sketch scratched beside the letters. Tuo said Crescent House sometimes sounded like several people arguing beneath a roof.

desert_p04_050.speaker: gao_ru
desert_p04_050.text: A duct can carry a voice far more easily than a room deserves. These old stations used shafts to draw cooler air through shaded walls. Broken edges turn some of them into whistles. We shall not open this one tonight; the masonry is loose and the sound is already explained well enough. Yue, sketch the visible outlet from here if you want it in your notes. Remember which way the wind blows. If you later hear a similar note at Crescent House, it may tell us where a shaft runs. It will not tell us who once stood beside it.

desert_p04_051.speaker: narrator
desert_p04_051.text: Du could now read two surviving characters above the stair: north and measure. The rest had flaked away. He resisted restoring a complete name from them, though Yue could see several candidates moving behind his expression. Instead he copied their shapes. His own earlier source described a chain of stations measuring wind, salt moisture, and caravan load. The buildings had lost official use when a northern road opened. Villagers had taken some roofs for repairs; travellers sheltered in the walls. The shelter's remaining duct was part of a practical system that had outlived its records by inconveniently continuing to work.

desert_p04_052.speaker: narrator
desert_p04_052.text: Yue drew the opening and added its note as she remembered it. Her little sketch looked like a bent spoon. Gao said the bend mattered more than beauty. Bao called her back to the lamp to replace the hand dressings with thinner wraps. The skin had closed enough for ordinary light work, provided she avoided abrasive grips. Yue flexed her fingers and felt the difference immediately. A small freedom could be as satisfying as the great stage she had earned under observation.

desert_p04_053.speaker: narrator
desert_p04_053.text: She folded the stained old dressing into Bao's waste packet rather than letting the basin collect another traveller's carelessness. Near the shelters Han found a new rope tied to the broken wall. A driver had hung his damp shirt from a projecting stone, intending to retrieve it before sleep. The wall lay beyond the camp's chosen fall zone, but the line crossed the path to the treatment corner. Han untied it and asked the man to use the cart rail. The driver grumbled that the shirt would dry more slowly there. A pebble fell where the rope had rubbed.

desert_p04_054.speaker: narrator
desert_p04_054.text: They both looked at it. Han handed over the shirt without a lecture, and the driver moved the line himself. The pebble seemed small until Yue imagined it above a sleeping face. She remembered the mason's hanging screen at the Black Gate and understood why he had insisted on waiting. In town, danger had often arrived alongside people employed to manage it. On the basin road, the crew had to keep their own chosen boundaries visible after fatigue and inconvenience softened them.

desert_p04_055.speaker: narrator
desert_p04_055.text: She moved her staff away from the stair wall so nobody would take its position as an invitation to approach. Gao noticed but offered no reward. The better place for the staff was simply beside its case. Tuo took Yue to the ridge edge before the last light disappeared. Far north, a red mast stood above a dark notch in the ground. It marked the next day's major junction and could be seen from a distance ordinary ground stones would never permit. Tuo had known it since her brother's earliest freight trips.

desert_p04_056.speaker: narrator
desert_p04_056.text: Its paint had been renewed, though not always by the people whose route it originally marked. She pointed out the notch itself as the more durable feature. The mast leaned slightly west. Yue sketched both, leaving the red colour to a word beside her pencil line.

desert_p04_057.speaker: tuo_yin
desert_p04_057.text: There are three approaches below that mast. One follows the public ridge. One goes down to the old wells, which are poor drinking places even when somebody leaves a handsome bucket beside them. The third crosses a salt shelf that saves distance in dry years. We shall look at the shelf before choosing. A guide who says she has crossed a place twenty times may mean only that nineteen years have gone by since she learned its worst habit. I want to see the dark seam at its edge.

desert_p04_058.speaker: tuo_yin
desert_p04_058.text: If it has widened, the public ridge earns another day of my affection.

desert_p04_059.speaker: narrator
desert_p04_059.text: Yue asked whether the mast was part of the old measurement stations. Tuo thought it had begun as a signal post for carts waiting below the notch. A red square meant the upper track was clear; a dark one meant wait. Nobody maintained that system now. The remaining paint marked a place, not a current instruction. Du, approaching behind them, confirmed the description from a former carrier's ledger. He had expected Tuo to disagree and looked pleased when she merely nodded. The three watched a bird land on the mast's crosspiece.

desert_p04_060.speaker: narrator
desert_p04_060.text: Its own tiny signal told them nothing useful beyond the existence of a perch. That night the camp worker's wrist woke him once. Bao replaced the binding and placed him where another person could manage his tent flap. Yue heard the exchange through cloth, then the quiet word of thanks. Wind sang briefly in the abandoned duct, higher than before. She recognised it and no longer imagined footsteps under the broken stair. The recognition did not diminish the loneliness of the sound. A machine could sing without intending anything, and people could hear their own history inside it.

desert_p04_061.speaker: narrator
desert_p04_061.text: She lay still until the note ended, letting the thought remain a thought instead of turning it into a report. Before dawn Gao asked the crew how they had slept. The camp worker's wrist was sore but improved; one driver had a headache that eased after breakfast and water. Bao kept him out of the first leading turn while she watched its return. They would travel earlier, not longer without another check. Han agreed, though his finger rested on the fourth-day arrival line in the plan. Tuo packed the route sheets separately from the ventilation notes.

desert_p04_062.speaker: narrator
desert_p04_062.text: Yue put the dry grass sample away beside the old road notice. Both had changed what she knew; neither needed to tell her where to walk. The caravan left the broken shelter while its wall still held a band of blue shadow. The singing duct stayed silent in the cooler air. Yue helped fold light guy lines, then carried the flag case beside the second cart until the track widened. Long Legs had taken the camp worker's hammer for the morning packing and complained that his dignity now weighed more than expected.

desert_p04_063.speaker: narrator
desert_p04_063.text: The worker said he would claim it back at the next camp if the driver proved unable to manage both. Their teasing concealed an ordinary gratitude that neither seemed ready to state plainly. The public ridge rose gently toward the red mast. Its outer edge held small black stones unlike the grey gravel farther south. Gao identified them as weathered volcanic fragments from the dark ridge, not proof of anything burning nearby. Yue turned one loose piece with her staff and saw a smooth interior face where it had broken. She left it in place.

desert_p04_064.speaker: narrator
desert_p04_064.text: The fish-shaped white stone remained a promise she might fulfil near a safe stopping place; collecting every interesting object would soon give her pack an education her shoulders could not support. Tuo approved the empty hands without asking their reason. An abandoned cart stood off the road before the junction, stripped of its wheels and covered in windblown salt. The body bore an old carrier mark Du recognised from a company closed years ago. Its broken rear beam showed a repair that had failed across the same grain. Han stopped to examine it, kneeling without touching the weakened frame.

desert_p04_065.speaker: narrator
desert_p04_065.text: He said the wheelwright in Bitter Wells would want a sketch of that joint. Yue drew it at his request. The old wreck offered a lesson without supplying a reliable story about its passengers. No bones, luggage, or fresh tracks remained around it. Tuo found a little stone shelter behind the wreck, likely built by travellers waiting for another team. Its floor lay above the nearest salt hollow. She checked the sightline to the mast and noted it for an emergency halt, not a planned source of supplies.

desert_p04_066.speaker: narrator
desert_p04_066.text: The cook peered inside, declared it large enough for three beans and a thin argument, and returned to his cart. Gao laughed. Han asked him whether he could cook for twelve in a place that size. The cook said certainly, provided eleven ate outside and the twelfth agreed never to move. At the first short rest Yue loosened her sandal strap before the blister pressed hard against it. Bao checked the protected patch and approved the adjustment. The girl felt absurdly proud of noticing discomfort while it was still small. The clinician let the pride stand.

desert_p04_067.speaker: narrator
desert_p04_067.text: Learning depended on recognitions that rarely made good stories around a fire. Nearby, the driver with the wooden bird tried its two notes under his breath. Plum turned one ear toward him, then away. The farrier announced that the animal's opinion was sufficiently clear and should not be written into the daughter's letter. By midmorning the mast's faded red cloth became visible beneath its crosspiece. It had been tied recently, though the staff itself was old. Tuo stopped at the lower notch to examine the ground before following its apparent direction. Three sets of cart tracks diverged there.

desert_p04_068.speaker: narrator
desert_p04_068.text: The freshest took the salt shelf, perhaps yesterday or the day before. Another followed the public ridge; the third ended near the old wells. Yue sketched their positions while Gao walked the safe verge. Freshness could identify recent use. It could not reveal whether the carts had returned, or whether the travellers had regretted going. Du found a notice nailed to the mast's lower post. Its printed heading offered a corrected short route to Crescent House, supplied by a northern carrier office. The date was recent enough to be tempting. A handwritten arrow pointed toward the salt shelf.

desert_p04_069.speaker: narrator
desert_p04_069.text: Tuo read it twice, then asked Han whether he recognised the office mark. He did. It belonged to one of the survey subscribers, the rival factor whose load had turned back. The man had promised new information after hiring a separate guide. Nobody had promised that the information would arrive as a paper nailed where weather could blur its conditions.

desert_p04_070.speaker: han_xun
desert_p04_070.text: I know the office, and I know the man can write a useful report when profit gives him reason. We shall read the whole sheet before calling it fraud or salvation. It may be perfectly sound for the loads that used it. Our tanks make a different cart. Gao, can you see whether the shelf's seam has widened? Tuo, take whatever time you need at the junction. Du, please stop holding the paper as though somebody has insulted your ancestors. It criticises your distance, not your family, unless there is a private footnote I have failed to notice.

desert_p04_071.speaker: narrator
desert_p04_071.text: Du lowered the notice enough for Gao to read. Its small print limited the route to light wagons following the southern edge. The arrow did not show that edge. A copied distance referred to the new cistern origin in Bitter Wells but the surrounding text used the old market start. Yue recognised the inconsistency from their first day's correction. She pointed without triumph. Du's mouth tightened at seeing the same error in a rival's paper. Gao asked him to retain that recognition when writing about his own sheet.

desert_p04_072.speaker: narrator
desert_p04_072.text: Tuo was already walking toward the seam, staff testing only the verge she could safely reach. The mast cloth fluttered as Tuo returned. The salt shelf carried a broad new crack near its northern side, damp beneath the crust. A light wagon keeping south might cross; loaded water carts should remain on the public ridge unless a fuller inspection proved otherwise. Gao agreed from what she had seen. Han folded the notice and copied its exact wording into the correspondence book. They would send the office a clarification rather than tearing away information some smaller travellers might still use.

desert_p04_073.speaker: narrator
desert_p04_073.text: Yue felt the wind lift her hat brim. The shorter road remained visible, bright and smooth, more attractive than the safer one. Long Legs looked down the salt shelf and said the last carriage tracks appeared convincing. Tuo asked him to compare their depth with his own wheel ruts. He crouched, saw the difference, and straightened reluctantly. Han chose the ridge. The driver accepted the choice, but his disappointment did not vanish. Yue understood it; her feet were also tired.

desert_p04_074.speaker: narrator
desert_p04_074.text: They had left the village's music behind to climb over rough gravel while a smooth white road promised the destination more quickly. Danger could tempt through comfort as readily as treasure. The cook covered the bowls and prepared to serve lunch on the less charming route. As they moved past the mast, Gao asked Yue to check that the third cart still saw the stopping flag. The road curved behind a black outcrop, narrowing the sightline. Yue walked back until the equipment driver could see her clearly.

desert_p04_075.speaker: narrator
desert_p04_075.text: Beyond the curve she glimpsed another red cloth tied low over the salt shelf's southern edge. It might mark the recommended line, or merely someone's warning. She called Tuo rather than deciding. The guide turned, looking first at the cloth and then at the distant tracks. For a moment her face lost its ordinary readiness to joke.

desert_p04_076.speaker: tuo_yin
desert_p04_076.text: That cloth has a black border. The northern office uses plain red. I know the weave, or think I do, and thinking is not enough. We shall stay on the ridge. Gao, take a look with the sighting glass from the firm shoulder. Tell me whether there is another cart beyond the rise. The notice may have brought somebody onto the shelf after its edge changed. I want to know whether we are looking at a marker tied neatly by a satisfied guide, or a piece of clothing somebody put where people might finally notice it.

desert_p04_077.speaker: narrator
desert_p04_077.text: Gao unpacked the ordinary sighting glass from her case and steadied it against the staff. Past the bordered cloth, the shelf dipped into a pale hollow. One wheel rose above its far lip, motionless, too isolated to belong to a cart travelling normally. She lowered the glass and told Han. Tuo went still, then pointed to the firm southern approach. They could inspect from there without sending all three carts onto the shelf. Yue held the red flag for the waiting drivers, feeling its small weight against her healing fingers.

desert_p04_078.speaker: narrator
desert_p04_078.text: Their planned road had acquired people they had not yet seen.
